title: Strat Chat – The Do Now
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien makes the case for opening every lesson with a Do Now, a short task students start the moment they enter the room. He describes his earlier habit of fighting for attention and recapping aloud, and explains that the Do Now works as both a behavioural routine and spaced retrieval practice. The question must retrieve content from previous lessons, not preview new content or interleave older material, so it can also serve as a diagnostic of what has been forgotten. He warns that hooking students with a question about new learning favours those with prior knowledge, and that easy questions waste the opportunity. He then compares four formats (mini whiteboards, booklets, short quizzes, think-pair-share) and says he mostly uses mini whiteboards for flexibility. Close call between this bucket and Practice and Culture; the retrieval and diagnostic purpose drove the call.
points: A Do Now combines a routine that sets expectations from the first second with retrieval practice, so it pays off in both behaviour and learning.
The task should retrieve what was learned in previous lessons, and using it to preview new content risks advantaging students who already know more.
The student work time frees three to ten minutes for roll, uniform checks and homework checks that would otherwise invite distraction.
Mini whiteboards, booklets, quizzes and think-pair-share each trade flexibility against evidence collection and depth.
quotes: There was once a time in my career where I would start every single lesson by battling to get the students attention. I would talk over some of them to verbally recap the prior lesson and then I would immediately launch into new content.
Equal parts behavioural routine and spaced retrieval practice, it gives a lot of bang for your buck. It sets the expectations high from the moment your students enter the classroom.
While they’re working the roll is complete, uniform is checked and homework is sighted and marked off. One small task sets big expectations for the students.

Yes, interleaved practice is important too, but this is not the time for it. This question also works as a diagnostic tool measuring how much of yesterday’s learning has been forgotten so that the following recap of prior learning can be tweaked to match the needs of your students before checking for understanding one more time before finally beginning new content.

Teacher beware: sometimes there can be temptations to use a Do Now as an opportunity to hook students in with an interesting question about the new learning. This is not the purpose of a Do Now and this lethal mutation risks benefitting the privileged students with existing prior knowledge and leaving our most vulnerable students starting the lesson feeling less than.

The upside here is that it creates a really strong routine and collects evidence of a students progress over time. It is important that these booklets remain in the classroom so you avoid any disruptions with “Miss/Sir I left my booklet at home”.
